verdict-inside: At this eye height the target is inside the horizon ({d0}), so the globe hides nothing either and the two models agree about the base. They still disagree about the angle — see the Elevation-angles tab. To make the hidden height the test, move further out or get lower.
verdict-whole: The globe hides more than the whole target ({H} of {h} m), so on a sphere nothing at all should show here on straight rays; {refrClause} A plane says the full {h} m is in view, base included, on any clear day. Verdict rule: photograph the base and the sphere is in serious trouble; photograph a summit floating free of its own coastline and the plane is.
verdict-whole-still: with k = {k} refraction still does not lift it clear.
verdict-whole-lifts: with k = {k} refraction lifts the top {visR} into view — which is exactly how such sightings are reported to work.
verdict-partial: Verdict rule: if the bottom {H} of this target is visible in still, cold air from a measured eye height of {e} m — reproducibly, and with the missing height staying at zero as d grows — the globe is refuted. If the base is cut off at about {Hr} and the cut retreats as you climb, the plane is. Zoom decides nothing here: magnification restores detail, never geometry.
tab-note: Computed live from the radius in the Elevation-angles tab (R = {R} km) and k = {k}. The “plane hides” column is not an approximation or a rounded value — it is exactly zero for every row, at every distance, for every observer height, because a plane has no bulge to hide anything behind. That column is the flat model's entire prediction, and it is the one column that cannot be adjusted.

exagg-capped: Requested {exReq}× was capped at {exMax}× — beyond that the target wraps around the far side of the reduced planet and the drawing stops meaning anything.

sweep-dv-globe: globe prediction at your height: {H} hidden ({Hr} with k = {k})
sweep-climb: climbing the whole ladder uncovers {delta} of the far base
sweep-verdict: Verdict rule: the flat model predicts that climbing changes the target's apparent size and position and nothing else — the same fraction of the base is visible from the sand and from 1,700 m, namely all of it. The globe predicts a specific slab returning at each step, set by d₀ = √(2Re) alone. If the base of a distant target looks identical from three well-separated heights on the same morning, the sphere is dead. If a measurable slab comes back each time you climb, and the amounts match the row above, the plane is — and R falls out of the numbers.
rec-note-lead: Ceiling = √(2R′h₁) + √(2R′h₂) with R′ = {Rg} km (R = {R} km, k = {k}). The closest any record has come is {worst}% of its own ceiling
rec-note-over-sing: , and {over} row is currently over it.
rec-note-over-plur: , and {over} rows are currently over it.
rec-note-refr-on: Untick refraction above and the top rows go past 100% — which is precisely the flat-earth calculation of this case, and precisely why omitting refraction is the error rather than the discovery.
rec-note-refr-off: Refraction is currently OFF, so these are straight-ray ceilings: the top records exceed them, which is the flat-earth calculation. Tick refraction above and every row falls back inside its limit at the standard k.
rec-note-tail: Nothing here is fitted: k is the value set by the refraction controls, the heights are the published ones, and the ceiling has no adjustable term.
